name: Qing Eight Banners and Green Standard army (1644-1799)

weightNotes.aggression: Conquest of Ming China (1644-83), the Dzungar wars and the Ten Great Campaigns of the 18th century, including four invasions of Burma (Eight Banners, Dzungar-Qing Wars, Sino-Burmese War pages). High.
weightNotes.maneuver: Manchu and Mongol banner cavalry could move fast (Shanhai Pass 1644 opened the road to Beijing), but the great steppe campaigns were slow logistical operations (Kangxi's 80-day trek across the Gobi in 1696, Jao Modo page). Middling.
weightNotes.flanking: Standard order put cannon and infantry in the centre and Manchu and Mongol cavalry on the flanks (Jao Modo page). No distinctive envelopment doctrine in the sources used. Middling.
weightNotes.siegePreference: Han Banner artillery decided the siege of Dalinghe (1631) and cannon were carried on camelback into the steppe (Eight Banners, Jao Modo pages); but the decisive objective in the Dzungar wars was the enemy field army. Balanced.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Banners were held as an emergency force behind the Green Standard garrisons, which 'actively military governed China locally' while bannermen 'were only brought into emergency situations' (Green Standard Army page). Moderate, educated guess at battle level.
weightNotes.scouting: Mongol allies and steppe intelligence served well against the Dzungars, but in Burma the army walked into the Bhamo-Kaungton trap and was encircled at Maymyo (Sino-Burmese War page). Middling.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Share of the engaged force lost before it withdrew or broke. Banner troops held until destroyed: Maymyo 1768, the encircled bannerman army fought three days and only 2,500 of 30,000 survived, as prisoners, about 92% lost (Sino-Burmese War page); Zhenjiang 1842, the 1,583 Manchu bannermen fought until overrun and then committed mass suicide (Zhenjiang page). Jao Modo 1696: the Qing centre 'began to collapse' but held and won (Jao Modo page). The Green Standard broke earlier, no figure. 0.6 for the banner core.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Manchu and Mongol mounted archers, Han Banner artillery and musketeers, and Green Standard infantry; at Jao Modo the Qing 'bombarded Dzungar troops with their cannons and then advanced behind a wooden barricade' with cavalry on the flanks (Jao Modo page).
weightNotes.initiative: Campaigns were directed by the emperor through palace memorials (Kangxi led in person in 1696); banner commanders had little latitude and failure was punished (Elliott, Manchu Way; Sino-Burmese War page). Low-middling.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Kangxi's 1696 expedition was preceded by 1,333 grain carts (Dzungar-Qing Wars page) and Perdue (China Marches West) shows that the state's logistical capacity is what finally beat the Dzungars. Burma was lost to disease and supply, not tactics. High.

summary: A hereditary military caste of Manchu, Mongol and Han bannermen, stipended and garrisoned, formed the elite strike force; the far larger Green Standard Army of former Ming troops garrisoned and policed the provinces. Banner cavalry kept Manchu mounted archery while Han bannermen manned artillery cast with Jesuit and defector help. The great campaigns against the Dzungars were won by logistics: grain convoys, depots and cannon carried across the Gobi, with the emperor directing from the capital or the field.
whyItWorked: The Qing fused steppe cavalry with Chinese artillery and the fiscal resources of China. That combination took Beijing after Shanhai Pass (1644), broke Galdan's army at Jao Modo (1696, Dzungar army 'bereft of artillery' broke under cannon and musket fire), and by the 1750s destroyed the Dzungar state and incorporated Xinjiang and Tibet.
whereItFailed: Outside the steppe and north China climate: the Burma invasions (1765-69) cost over 70,000 Qing soldiers, mostly to disease, and the main banner army was annihilated at Maymyo (1768). After the Ten Great Campaigns banner quality declined, and against an industrial navy the system failed entirely (First Opium War, Zhenjiang 1842).

sources.title: Perdue, China Marches West: The Qing Conquest of Central Eurasia (Harvard UP, 2005)
Elliott, The Manchu Way: The Eight Banners and Ethnic Identity in Late Imperial China (Stanford UP, 2001)
Graff and Higham (eds.), A Military History of China (UP of Kentucky, 2012)
